title: MOS 6502 instruction encoding
summary: The MOS 6502 is an 8-bit microprocessor (1975) used in the Apple II, Commodore 64, NES, and Atari 2600. Instructions are 1-3 bytes. Addressing modes: immediate (#), zero page (zp), zero page X/Y (zp,X/Y), absolute (abs), absolute X/Y (abs,X/Y), indirect (ind), indirect X/Y ((ind,X), (ind),Y), relative (rel, for branches). 3 registers: A (accumulator), X, Y (index). Status flags: N (negative), V (overflow), B (break), D (decimal), I (interrupt disable), Z (zero), C (carry).

structure.meaning: Opcode (1 byte) + optional operand (0, 1, or 2 bytes). No prefixes, no ModR/M.

Immediate (#imm), Zero Page (zp), Zero Page X (zp,X), Zero Page Y (zp,Y), Absolute (abs), Absolute X (abs,X), Absolute Y (abs,Y), Indirect (ind), Indirect X ((ind,X)), Indirect Y ((ind),Y), Relative (rel, for branches).
A (accumulator), X (index), Y (index). Plus SP (stack pointer, 8-bit, page 1: 0x0100-0x01FF), PC (program counter, 16-bit), P (status register, 8 bits).
Bit 7 N (negative), 6 V (overflow), 5 (unused, always 1), 4 B (break), 3 D (decimal mode), 2 I (interrupt disable), 1 Z (zero), 0 C (carry).
16-bit address space (0x0000-0xFFFF). Zero page (0x00-0xFF) for fast access.

notes: The 6502 is one of the most influential 8-bit CPUs.
6502 uses zero-page addressing for fast 8-bit address access.
6502 has no multiply/divide instructions (done in software).
6502's decimal mode (D flag) enables BCD arithmetic.
The 6502's simple design made it cheap and ubiquitous (Apple II, C64, NES).
